title: Coles profit hit by wage underpayment scandal
excerpt: Coles chief executive Leah Weckert said it had been another steady year of results for the supermarket, weighed down by the cost of paying workers what they were owed.
body:
Coles reported its full-year results this week, with profit weighed down by the cost of the wage underpayment scandal that has been winding through the courts. Chief executive Leah Weckert said it had been 'another consistent set of results' for the supermarket, with the wage recovery costs now a permanent part of the business, not a one-off.

Our take: this is the latest in a string of large-employer underpayment scandals. Woolworths, Bunnings, Caltex, 7-Eleven, George Calombaris's Made Establishment, and now Coles. The pattern is clear: these are not isolated payroll mistakes, they are systematic failures of payroll systems in big companies that have been getting the award rates wrong for years. The Fair Work Ombudsman, the government body that handles wage disputes, has been stepping up prosecutions, and the penalties now include back-pay of up to ten years, plus fines.

For workers, the upside is that the regulator is finally catching up. For investors, the underpayment cost is now a permanent line in the company's accounts, not a one-off, and it deserves to be built into every large-employer valuation.

The most under-reported detail: most of the underpaid workers were casual or part-time, paid at the base award rate but missing the higher weekend rates, public holiday rates, or late-night rates they were entitled to. If you work in retail, hospitality, or fast food, and you have not checked your payslips against the award in the last twelve months, do it now.

In plain terms: the underpayment problem is bigger than Coles. If your pay has ever felt a bit off, the Fair Work Ombudsman has a free calculator and a free complaints process. The window to claim goes back further than most people realise.
whatItMeans: If you work in retail, hospitality, or fast food: Check your payslips against the relevant award, the legal minimum pay and conditions for your job, using the Fair Work Ombudsman's free pay calculator. The Fair Work Ombudsman can order your employer to back-pay you up to ten years for award breaches, and up to six years for breaches of your employment contract.
If you are a Coles or Woolworths shareholder: Underpayment costs are now a normal part of doing business, not a one-off surprise. Build them into your valuation model.
If you are a hiring manager at a large employer: Treat payroll as a legal risk, not just an HR function. The cost of getting it wrong now exceeds the cost of an audit.
If you think you have been underpaid in the past: The Fair Work Ombudsman complaints process is free. The window to claim goes back further than most people realise.
